episode_title: 94. Human irrationality & Behavioural Economics with prof. Kirchler

recommendations.speaker: Markus Gedda

recommendations.quote: So, my tip is to do some research on that company. Yeah. There's a thin tweed stock right now that's going bananas.

insights.quote: one major lesson from behavioral finance is that overconfidence is not good for individual investors. So there are some studies showing that those investors that trade much more than others, that after costs, they have a lower end return than those investors that have a buy and hold strategy almost because they hardly trade. And the difference is that before costs, the returns of these two groups are almost identical and after costs, after the trading costs, and this is of course much that they are of course much higher for those that trade a lot. The returns of the high traders or the high frequency traders are clearly lower, significantly lower than those of the passive investors.
insights.summary: High trading frequency leads to lower returns after costs; passive buy-and-hold strategies outperform active trading due to transaction expenses.
insights.speaker: Michael Kirchler

insights.quote: The easiest thing to do is probably just to invest in some passive index fund and just live life. Yeah, but you save monthly and then you will buy both when it's high, but also when it's low, definitely.
insights.summary: Monthly passive index fund investing across market cycles eliminates timing risk and provides consistent returns.
insights.speaker: Tim Hansson

insights.quote: as a private investor, try to have a mid or long term perspective of 10, 15, 20 years and go well diversified, broadly diversified in different index products and do not trade much because this will always harm your net performance, the trading costs. They are evil.
insights.summary: Long-term perspective of 10-20 years with broad diversification and minimal trading is the optimal approach for private investors.
insights.speaker: Michael Kirchler

insights.quote: loss aversion means our tendency that we value losses more strongly than we value gains. So for instance, losing 1000 Swiss Kroner hurts me much more than getting an additional 1000 Kroner. So even in experiments, for instance, if you run those experiments where people are offered to lose 200 Kroner or they can win 300 Kroner. So the expected value is positive actually. Then most people will reject this gamble because the minus 200, the potential that they lose 200, weights more than the additional gain of 300.
insights.summary: Humans feel losses about twice as strongly as equivalent gains, leading to irrational rejection of positive expected value gambles.
insights.speaker: Michael Kirchler

insights.quote: confirmation bias, I think, is really evil because, especially nowadays with social media and so on, this can lead to those filter bubbles and to conspiracy theories, because if you take a wrong turn as an individual and go through those conspiracy theories, you will always find some stories that confirm with your strange theory, and you still believe and it makes you even more confident that this is true.
insights.summary: Confirmation bias combined with social media creates filter bubbles and reinforces false beliefs, making it dangerous for investors.
insights.speaker: Michael Kirchler

insights.quote: I think it's sad if they enter the market at the peak and then they leave at the bottom. That would be the worst thing to do. Of course, now you want to sit tight and maybe purchase even more.
insights.summary: Buying at market peaks and selling at bottoms is the worst possible strategy; staying invested or buying more during downturns is preferable.
insights.speaker: Michael Kirchler

insights.quote: And this was just pretty crazy time, especially in Europe, because there were these tech companies popping up, and quite a lot of private investors entered the market for the first time. And during 1998, 1999, almost all of the tech stocks, no matter which business model was in the background, were increasing in price. And I was also thrilled. I found it interesting. I was at the beginning of my university studies, and then I invested a little bit. Fortunately, I did not have so much money. Which prevented me from doing too many stupid things.
insights.summary: Market bubbles often involve inexperienced investors entering during late stages; having limited capital can protect investors from making large mistakes.
insights.speaker: Michael Kirchler

insights.quote: one factor is if all of a sudden a lot of new investors enter the market for some reason, because all of a sudden they realize, oh, there's a party going on and my neighbor already made some money, I should invest as well. Even without knowing what a stock is. This is one of the historical reasons why bubbles emerge. So simply demand pressure and therefore prices are built up pretty strongly. And this was one of the reasons for the dot-com bubble that a herd of inexperienced traders all of a sudden entered the market.
insights.summary: Bubbles often form when inexperienced investors herd into the market due to FOMO, creating unsustainable demand pressure.
insights.speaker: Michael Kirchler

insights.quote: If you make 6 or 8 percent per year return, on average, that's a lot. But the 1.2 or 2 percent of commissions or management fee, that's already a quarter of your annual return. That's a lot if you think about that. Because 1.5 percent doesn't sound that much per year, but it's around a quarter of what you can expect in return or in performance every year, and that's insane. And this makes you basically dead after 20 or 30 years, because then you have, I think, your final portfolio value after 30 years will probably be around 40 or 50 percent of what you would have without management fee.
insights.summary: Management fees of 1.5-2% consume about 25% of expected returns and can reduce final portfolio value by 50-60% over 30 years.
insights.speaker: Michael Kirchler

insights.quote: And I think even in the recession, yeah, maybe they will save out on something else instead. Maybe they save on nutrition, that they buy the cheap food. I'd rather starve myself than sell my Louboutin.
insights.summary: People prioritize status signaling during recessions, often cutting back on essentials rather than luxury goods that maintain social status.
insights.speaker: Markus Gedda

summary: This episode features Professor Michael Kirchler discussing behavioral finance and investment psychology. The conversation covers topics like market bubbles, anchoring effects, loss aversion, confirmation bias, and probability weighting. Kirchler shares research on how irrational human behavior affects financial decisions, using examples from the dot-com bubble and recent market cycles. The episode emphasizes the importance of passive index fund investing over active trading, the detrimental impact of management fees, and the difficulty of spotting bubbles in real-time. The hosts discuss the energy market situation in Europe, particularly gas supply issues, and briefly mention a few stocks including Grodno (heat pumps) and Tingstaden (real estate rights issue) in the closing segment.
key_takeaways: Passive index fund investing with long-term horizons outperforms active trading due to transaction costs
Loss aversion makes people irrationally avoid even positive expected value gambles
Confirmation bias leads to filter bubbles and reinforces false beliefs
Management fees of 1.5-2% can reduce portfolio value by 50% over 30 years
Market bubbles often emerge when inexperienced investors herd in due to FOMO
Spotting bubbles in real-time is extremely difficult due to vague definitions
The energy market price increases are driven by supply-demand fundamentals, not speculation
Trial offers exploit loss aversion by making giving up a product feel like a loss
